faqs.a: Analogous colors sit next to each other on the color wheel (for example blue, blue-violet and violet). Because they share a hue family, they look calm and unified. Complementary colors sit opposite each other and create strong contrast instead.
faqs.q: What is the difference between analogous and complementary schemes?

faqs.a: A 30-degree spread is the classic choice — close enough to feel related, far enough to stay distinguishable. Use 10–20 degrees for subtle, elegant palettes and 40–60 degrees for more energetic ones.

faqs.q: Why do the four neighbor colors look related?

howTo: Pick your base color with the color picker or type its HEX code.
Move the spread slider to widen or narrow the scheme (10 to 60 degrees).
Review the five swatches and the gradient strip preview.
Click the copy button on any swatch to copy its HEX code.
Paste the codes into your CSS, Figma or presentation.
keyFacts: Analogous colors occupy neighboring positions on the color wheel.
This tool builds five swatches: the base plus two neighbors on each side.
Saturation and lightness are kept identical to the base color; only the hue changes.
The spread slider controls how far apart the neighbors sit (10 to 60 degrees).
All hue math wraps around 0/360 degrees, so red neighbors work correctly.

analogous-color-scheme.tagline: Build a harmonious five-color palette from any base color — neighbors on the color wheel, ready to copy.
analogous-color-scheme.workedExample:
Take base color #4f46e5.
Its hue is about 243 degrees, with 75% saturation and 59% lightness.
With a 30-degree spread the five swatch hues are 243 - 60 = 183, 243 - 30 = 213, 243, 243 + 30 = 273 and 243 + 60 = 303 degrees.
Saturation (75%) and lightness (59%) stay the same, so all five swatches share the same intensity and brightness — only the hue shifts.
